newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel votes down J&J prostate drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel votes down J&J prostate drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Tuesday voted against approval of Janssen Pharmaceutica's liarozole fumarate (Liazal) as a second-line treatment for advanced prostate cancer.
The disease kills 42,000 American men a year.
Janssen, a division of Johnson and Johnson, applied for FDA approval for Liazal in December 1996.
In an unusual move, Janssen pleaded for approval saying there were not enough treatment options for advanced disease.

Panelists were not receptive. Committee member David Johnson of Vanderbilt University Medical School disputed the company's assertion that the drug improved quality of life or otherwise helped patients, saying "The ultimate cynic would say that you demonstrated that Liazal causes harm."

Panel members and FDA reviewers criticized the design of the two pivotal Janssen studies, saying that the company had revised the data after the studies' completion. Panelists also noted that in both studies, Liazal was not shown to be superior to the drug it was compared to.

Janssen presented data from two pivotal phase III trials. In the first, 117 patients taking Liazal were compared to 103 patients taking prednisone, an oral corticosteroid. The primary goal was to increase survival. Those taking Liazal survived a median 11.7 months, compared to 15.8 months for patients taking prednisone.
The second study used international data -- 260 patients taking Liazal were compared to 161 patients taking cyproterone acetate (CPA), a drug that has not been approved in the U.S.
In that study, Liazal patients survived a median 312 days, compared to 314 days for CPA patients.

FDA reviewers said that in both pivotal studies, CPA and prednisone not only had better survival rates, but also seemed to be better tolerated. Liazal patients had more nausea and vomiting -- about half in both trials experienced the side effects, compared to 13 percent of the prednisone patients and 34 percent of the CPA patients.

Possibly as a result of that, in both studies, close to one third of Liazal patients took less than 90 percent of the recommended dose. Patients also experienced skin problems such as repeated rashes.

The agency was also concerned about fluid retention in the lungs and congestive heart failure (CHF). In each trial, 10 Liazal patients had CHF, compared to three prednisone, and four CPA patients. Janssen said that it did not feel that the CHF was drug related, and said it could be due to a number of factors, including age and other conditions.
The panel was not convinced, however, and said that toxicity was a concern. FDA is not bound by the panel's advice but usually follows it.
